final.title: Design scope creep out before the build starts
final.body:
Scope creep is usually a sign that the workflow was never bounded properly. If you want to automate something in a small business, start with one recurring workflow and one clear measure. Ask: what repeats, where does the handoff happen, and how will you know it worked?

That is the decision point. If the work is repeatable, has a visible handoff, and can be measured, it is a pilot candidate. If it depends on open-ended judgment or keeps changing every week, keep it manual for now. Don’t let a useful idea become three other ideas wearing the same coat.

In Bareni’s normal sequence, the diagnostic identifies one recurring workflow, checks honestly whether AI fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures. The point is not to squeeze everything into the first build. The point is to make the boundary visible before anyone starts building.

If a new request appears mid-build, treat it as a separate workflow, not an informal add-on. Put it in the next conversation, not inside the current scope. That keeps the decision human and the scope inspectable.

Practical next step: write down one workflow you repeat every week, plus the success measure you would actually use for it. Then bring that into the diagnostic and decide whether it is a pilot or a manual task for now.

final.title: Design scope creep out before the build starts
final.body:
Scope creep usually starts when a small business treats one workflow as if it were three. The fix is not to be stricter for its own sake. It is to define the boundary before build starts.

For a workflow automation pilot, I’d keep it to one recurring task, one owner, and one success measure. The diagnostic question is simple: what is the one workflow that repeats, costs time, or creates risk, and how will you know it improved?

That question matters because it stops the conversation from drifting into adjacent work. If the owner starts adding a second workflow mid-build, or asks for a nice-to-have that belongs elsewhere, the answer is: that is a separate workflow. Put it in the next pilot, not this one.

The practical next step is to write down one weekly workflow in plain English, then attach a measurable outcome you already care about. For example: customer questions answered within a set time, or invoices logged within a set time. Those are examples of what to measure, not promises.

Bareni’s working rule is boring on purpose: small scope, written boundary, human approval kept in the loop. That is usually enough to make the decision visible before anyone starts building.
